title: Empirical development of the Volitional Apathy Scale: A brief measure of behavioral initiation and maintenance.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Apathy, a clinical symptom commonly found in many brain conditions, is characterized by quantitative reductions in goal-directed behavior. Although apathy is widely conceptualized as multidimensional, existing measures vary in how its behavioral aspect is operationalized, limiting precision in the assessment of initiation and maintenance of goal-directed behavior. This study aimed to develop and validate a brief, behaviorally specific measure of apathy that addresses this inconsistency by capturing observable reductions in initiation and maintenance of goal-directed behavior.
METHOD: Candidate items were systematically reviewed from established scales against a behavior-focused operational definition of apathy. Six items proceeded to exploratory factor analysis in a mixed sample of individuals with neurodegenerative brain disorders and healthy controls (Sample 1;= 173). Confirmatory factor analysis was subsequently conducted in an independent, transdiagnostic clinical sample including neurological and psychiatric conditions (Sample 2;= 148). Reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity were examined using well-established functional, motivational, and cognitive measures.
RESULTS: The scale development process resulted in a parsimonious, four-item "Volitional Apathy Scale" with a unidimensional structure. The scale demonstrated good model fit, acceptable-to-strong internal consistency across samples (α = .75-.88; ω = .76-.88), and robust convergent validity with independent measures, controlling for the effects of age, education, and global cognition.
CONCLUSIONS: The Volitional Apathy Scale is a brief measure of the behavioral expression of apathy, capturing observable reductions in the initiation and maintenance of goal-directed activity. The scale offers a precise, parsimonious, and psychometrically supported transdiagnostic tool for apathy assessment in clinical and research contexts.
